hypothesis: If boys' and girls' growth velocity curves are similar in shape but differ in phase and amplitude, the female curve is closely matched by a time-shifted male curve, with the female adolescent acceleration earlier.
pass_criterion: Female and male mean velocity curves (from NHANES, ages 4–18) correlate with r ≥ 0.8 after the best time shift. The female peak velocity age is 1.5–3 years earlier than the male one, and the peak amplitudes differ by at least 5%.
fail_criterion: The best-shift correlation is below 0.6, or the female peak is not earlier than the male one.
interpretation: 'Phase' is read as the age of peak velocity and take-off. 'Amplitude' is read as the peak velocity in cm/yr. NHANES is cross-sectional, so velocity is estimated by differencing smoothed mean stature by sex.

dataset.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES)
dataset.publisher: US National Center for Health Statistics, CDC
dataset.why_it_fits: Measured standing height with age and sex lets mean stature by age be computed separately for boys and girls, from which velocity curves are derived.
